summary: Specifies how IPv6 packets are carried over ARCnet networks: the frame format, how link-local and automatically configured IPv6 addresses are formed, and the link-layer address option used in IPv6 neighbor discovery messages. It was later updated by RFC 8064.

plainLanguage.summary: ARCnet is an old kind of office network. This document explains how to put new-style internet messages (IPv6) into its envelopes, and how each computer makes up its own address.

subtitle: How IPv6 packets travel over ARCnet: frame type, MTU, address formation and the neighbor discovery option.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needs link-specific rules before it can run on ARCnet, a network with only 8-bit hardware addresses and one multicast address.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns IPv6 the ARCnet protocol ID C4 hexadecimal, sets a default MTU of 9072 octets, builds interface identifiers from an EUI-64 or the 8-bit ARCnet address, and defines the link-layer address option for ARCnet.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 2497 is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the RFC Specifies
sections.content: RFC 2497 specifies a frame format for sending IPv6 packets over ARCnet and the way to form IPv6 link-local and statelessly autoconfigured addresses there. It also defines the Source/Target Link-layer Address option used by the Router Solicitation, Router Advertisement, Neighbor Solicitation, Neighbor Advertisement and Redirect messages of RFC 2461 when they are sent on an ARCnet.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a short rulebook for using the new internet addressing on one particular old kind of network.

sections.title: Frame Format and Protocol ID
sections.content:
IPv6 packets are fragmented and reassembled at the link layer according to the ARCNET Packet Header Definition Standard. A short description of the method is in RFC 1201, the IPv4 over ARCNET specification.

The protocol ID, called the System Code in ARCnet terms, assigned to IPv6 is C4 hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Big messages are cut into pieces for the network and glued back together at the other end. A special code, C4, tells the receiver the pieces hold IPv6.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
The largest IPv6 packet this encapsulation can carry is 60480 octets. That is impractical because the worst-case transmission time is several seconds, so all implementations on a given ARCnet should agree on a smaller value. The default MTU is 9072 octets.

With a router present, the MTU MAY be changed by a Router Advertisement carrying an MTU option. If the advertised MTU is larger than 60480, or larger than a manually configured value below 60480, it may be logged but MUST otherwise be ignored. With no router, the MTU MUST stay at 9072 or be manually set to the same value on all connected stations.

Implementations MAY accept arriving datagrams larger than their configured MTU. If they cannot handle them, they MAY log the event and MUST otherwise silently discard them.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages have a size limit, like a box that only holds so much. Everyone on the network should use the same box size, or the bigger boxes get thrown away.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
If a node has an EUI-64 not used for another interface, it SHOULD use it for its ARCnet interface. If that EUI-64 serves another interface on a different link, it MAY be reused. The Interface Identifier is the EUI-64 with the Universal/Local bit complemented.

With no EUI-64, the node MUST follow Appendix A of RFC 2373: the 8-bit manually configured ARCnet address is appended to 56 zero bits. For the address 49 hexadecimal this gives 56 zero bits followed by 01001001, which leaves the universal/local bit at 0 for local scope.

A prefix used for stateless autoconfiguration (RFC 2462) on ARCnet MUST be 64 bits long. The link-local address is the prefix FE80::/64 followed by the Interface Identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer with a serial number built into its card uses that to make its address. If it has none, it uses the small number someone set by hand and fills the rest with zeros.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content:
Unicast mapping follows RFC 2461. On ARCnet the Source/Target Link-layer Address option has a Type (1 for source, 2 for target), a Length of 1 (in units of 8 octets), the 8-bit ARCnet address in canonical bit order, and 5 octets of padding.

ARCnet offers only one multicast address, 00 hexadecimal, so all IPv6 multicast addresses MUST be mapped to it.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a neighbor, a computer asks for its hardware number, which is just one small byte here. Every group message goes to the one shared address that ARCnet has for groups.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Deriving Interface Identifiers from ARCnet addresses is intended to preserve local uniqueness where possible. The RFC notes that there is no protection from duplication through accident or forgery.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing stops two computers from picking the same address, by mistake or on purpose.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: 1 for source, 2 for target link-layer address.

fields.name: ARCnet address
fields.desc: The 8-bit ARCnet address, in canonical bit order.
